blocks.cap: The walk home with a stranger's tools in his hands

blocks.p: Okada took Kuga back to the grey block in a taxi, the carrier on her knees and the cat inside it sulking like a wet king, and Rei walked home along the canal. The trains had stopped. And a man with what was in his hands should not be underground, packed in with other people, until he understood what he was carrying.

The marks settled as he walked. That was the word for it. Settled, the way silt settles, the way a tenant settles, the way a thing that is on a person becomes a thing that is in him while he is busy thinking about something else. By the second bridge he could no longer feel the difference between reaching with his own thinned sight and reaching with the borrowed grain, so he made himself stop reaching at all. He jammed his hands into his pockets and kept them there.

It did not help much. On the third bridge a drunk had left an empty can on the rail. Rei flinched at a car horn, and the can slid away from him along the rail and dropped into the water, though his hand was nowhere near it. Telekinesis. Force with no hand behind it, the most visible thing a practitioner can do. He stood looking at the ripples and thought of every page in Gin's book that said the people who could do that learned to hide young, the first time a cup moved at the dinner table.

Under the expressway a streetlamp brightened as he passed beneath it, too bright, humming like a struck wire, and went out. The vending machine beside it stuttered its lights and reset. Rei walked faster. Somewhere a power log had just recorded a spike, and somewhere a camera had just lost three seconds. Psychokinesis did not leave a trail of footprints. It left a trail of paperwork.

By the river stairs his scraped heel stopped stinging. He looked down at it under a lantern. The graze had closed over, pink and new. A moment later the cold came, a deep tiredness like the floor of a long day, and he had to sit on the step until his hands stopped shaking. Healing was not free. It took what it used from the one doing it. Psychometabolism, and he had spent something of himself to mend a scratch he had not even minded.

He sat on the step and counted, because Gin had taught him to count things. The old woman's thought by the pool. The jump along the edge of the water. The can. The lamp. The heel. Five paths that were not his, firing one after another like a house settling at night. Six, with the Clairsentience he had always had. Every path there was. He had touched a man who had all of them lit at once, and the man's warmth had come home on his hands like flour.

He understood the shape of the next month then. The gifts would be useful exactly as far as they were dangerous. Every time the far shore's tools solved a problem for him, they would have solved it a little more as him and a little less as borrowing. And the Healer was in no hurry, because it did not need to be. It had forty years of patience behind it. Rei had two paths and an open wound that already, faintly, fit his palm.

He thought about Gin then, which he had not let himself do since the concrete, and he let himself think about him the true way and not the brave way. Gin was in there, leaning on the wall Rei had just touched the far side of. Gin was being worn by the thing that had wanted Rei to touch it. And the cruellest arithmetic of the whole crossing was this. The gift in his hands was the best tool he had ever had for finding his brother. It was also the leash the far shore was using to walk him toward his brother's chair. Sitting on a river step with his fists in his pockets, he could not tell whether wanting to use it to reach Gin was love, or the marks already learning to want what the seat wanted. All month he had been certain that whatever else was true, he was the one in his own head. He was no longer certain. And that, he understood, was exactly the instalment the far shore had meant to send home. Not a power. A doubt. The one wound a witness cannot read his way out of.

By his own door, the real one, the one that locked itself, the one this whole month had begun behind, he had made the only decision the night would let him make. It was not what to do with the gifts. It was whether to be honest that he had them.

The kitchen was dark through the glass. The kettle was cold. The chair across the table was empty in the small ordinary way, not the loud far-shore way. Rei stood on his own step with a stranger's tools printed into his hands, and his brother's body somewhere on the wrong side of a wall that rang like this room, and he knew that whatever he did next would decide what kind of person reached Gin when he finally reached him. The brother who went in. Or the thing the going-in was making.

Things that hide what they are have a way of becoming what they hide. He had watched it all month, in a cardigan, across this table. So he went in and switched on the light and sat down in his own chair, and he opened Gin's book to the back, and he wrote it at the top of a clean page in plain words before he could make them gentler. I went through at Senju. I touched it. I came back with things in my hands that are not mine. I am writing this down so I can't pretend later that I didn't know. In the morning he would tell Okada, and Itsuki, and anyone else who needed to know what was standing in their kitchen. Tonight he would tell the book.

Then, because Gin's book was the only map he had, he turned back to the addendum on Font proximity. He had read it the night after the cold room, when it was about other people. The four weights, Light and Moderate and Heavy and Critical. The weight is set at the instant of expulsion, and what follows is just time. It read differently now.

The bleed was there, the doubled edges of the kitchen, the hum of the neighbour's sleep through the wall that he had never been able to hear before. That was Light, weeks of it, and then the membrane would close. Then he thought of the snake striking at nothing over the grave-earth, and of Okada's fingers on its back. Something over there has your smell now. The line under Moderate said things contact them. He wrote Light in the margin, small, and after a long moment he wrote maybe more beside it.

It should have been worse. He had stood closer to the centre than anyone in the restricted files and walked home on his own feet. The reason was on the family page, the one where Gin had admitted to opening four paths in secret. Gin had come back from the Threshold at twenty-two lighter than he had any right to, and he had found the same thing in two Uedera ancestors' case files. His guess, written very carefully, was that a practitioner with more than one path open spreads the weight of the expulsion across all of them, so that no single path takes the blow. Two paths. The searching one and the nameless one under it, held flat since before he could read. They had split the blow between them. Gin had hidden them from the registry and taught him to hold them as a family habit, and tonight it had probably saved his mind.

Further down the same page Gin had written his advice to anyone thrown back. Find someone who has been there. Do not decide permanence from a bad week. And the fourth one, the one Gin had boxed in pencil.

Do not go back because the wanting says to. Rei put his finger on the line and held it there. Even now, with the light on and the kettle cold, he could feel the slope three hundred metres to the northeast, warm and patient, and the part of him that had stood at the top of it wanted very badly to go and lie down at the bottom. He took his finger off the page. He turned to the clean sheet where he had written his confession, and below it, in the order they had come to him, he wrote down the rest of what he had carried back.

doc.title: The back of Gin's book, in Rei's hand
lines: A paper lantern at dusk with 逢魔時 on it. Ōmagatoki. The hour when you meet demons. A crest under it like an office seal. An office? Of what?
A notebook full of names written small. Ink on the second finger. He asked questions for a living. Like Gin.
Wooden bridges, swords, no wires. Old. Edo? Before Tokyo was Tokyo.
A road at evening. He walked with his shadow beside him. Did not cut it off. Did not follow it. Down the middle.
A plain chair. He sat down in it and the weight came on. He did not get up. The Duty chair. He was in it first.
要. Pivot. Keystone. The pin a fan turns on. Why did he give me this?

blocks.p: He looked at the last line for a long time. Gin had said the chair needed its old one. Gin had said the whole registered world had put him somewhere. And the man at the centre had not been able to tell Rei who he was, only hand him pieces, the way a person hands over the contents of his pockets to someone he hopes will know what they mean.
Rei traced the character again, slowly, pressing hard enough to dent the page. 要. It did not look like a word. It looked like something a man might once have answered to.

The window was going grey. Somewhere in the walls the building's pipes knocked as the first neighbour ran a tap. Rei sat at the kitchen table where everything had started, and for the first time since Gin went quiet on that Wednesday night, he was not only trying to find his brother. He was trying to remember someone else's name.
